pages.text: 1 Case summary 10 March 2016 Further fines imposed in rail case Sector: Manufacturers and suppliers of track superstructure (rails, switches and sleepers) Ref.: B12 – 16/12, B12 – 19/12 Termination of proceedings: March 2016 In July 2013 and March 2016, the Bundeskartellamt imposed further fines totalling more than 100 million euros against nine undertakings in the rail cartel case. The fines were directed at price, quota and customer protection agreements to the detriment of local transport companies, private, regional and industrial railways and construction companies between 2001 and May 2011. Fines were imposed on ThyssenKrupp GfT Gleistechnik GmbH, Essen (88 million euros), voestalpine BWG GmbH, Butzbach (6.4 million euros) and Schreck-Mieves GmbH, Braunschweig (2.0 million euros). Fines totalling 1.24 million euros were imposed on the companies Holz-Fehlings Gleistechnik und Entsorgung GmbH, Marl-Sinsen, Fehlings Narosch Gleistechnik und Entsorgung GmbH, Munich, Künstler Bahntechnik GmbH, Holzwickede, Heinrich Krug GmbH & Co. KG, Dortmund, and Betzler Eisenbahntechnik GmbH, Aalen. These fines are meanwhile final In March 2016 one last fine amounting to 3.4 million euros was imposed on Vossloh Laeis GmbH, Trier. This fine has been appealed and is not yet binding. Nearly all the companies mentioned above cooperated with the Bundeskartellamt in the course of the proceedings within the scope of its leniency programme. In calculating the fines, based on its new fine guidelines, the Bundeskartellamt took into account the cooperation of the companies, the varying length of their cartel involvement and their willingness to terminate the proceedings by settlement. pages.text_long: 1 Case summary 10 March 2016 Further fines imposed in rail case Sector: Manufacturers and suppliers of track superstructure (rails, switches and sleepers) Ref.: B12 – 16/12, B12 – 19/12 Termination of proceedings: March 2016 In July 2013 and March 2016, the Bundeskartellamt imposed further fines totalling more than 100 million euros against nine undertakings in the rail cartel case. The fines were directed at price, quota and customer protection agreements to the detriment of local transport companies, private, regional and industrial railways and construction companies between 2001 and May 2011. Fines were imposed on ThyssenKrupp GfT Gleistechnik GmbH, Essen (88 million euros), voestalpine BWG GmbH, Butzbach (6.4 million euros) and Schreck-Mieves GmbH, Braunschweig (2.0 million euros). Fines totalling 1.24 million euros were imposed on the companies Holz-Fehlings Gleistechnik und Entsorgung GmbH, Marl-Sinsen, Fehlings Narosch Gleistechnik und Entsorgung GmbH, Munich, Künstler Bahntechnik GmbH, Holzwickede, Heinrich Krug GmbH & Co. KG, Dortmund, and Betzler Eisenbahntechnik GmbH, Aalen. These fines are meanwhile final In March 2016 one last fine amounting to 3.4 million euros was imposed on Vossloh Laeis GmbH, Trier. This fine has been appealed and is not yet binding. Nearly all the companies mentioned above cooperated with the Bundeskartellamt in the course of the proceedings within the scope of its leniency programme. In calculating the fines, based on its new fine guidelines, the Bundeskartellamt took into account the cooperation of the companies, the varying length of their cartel involvement and their willingness to terminate the proceedings by settlement. The rail cartel proceedings were originally triggered by an application for leniency filed by the company voestalpine in 2011. 2 The aim of the agreements was to divide up tenders or projects among the members of the cartel. The tenders generally included product combinations comprising several lots (rails of different qualities and profile types, switches and sleepers), but also individual lots. Where tenders involved several lots, agreements were coordinated by a rail or switch company, regardless of whether the project focused more on rails or switches. That ensured that collusion always took place on projects as a whole, regardless of their respective product focus. Not all the companies involved in the agreements offered all the products concerned and/or operated throughout Germany. However, while their levels of intensity varied in different regions, the cartel agreements were always based on the same basic understanding and similar implementation. Communication within the cartel took place mainly in telephone calls, personal meetings and emails. Price information was sometimes disguised on the telephone as share or stock market values. Sometimes, the prices were communicated as lottery numbers. These collusive practices in the private market were based on the classification of individual companies as “long-standing customers" or regular clients. This allocation of customers to particular companies was respected by the cartel members in principle. They “protected" these companies by consciously refraining from bidding, bidding only after the deadline had expired or submitting intentionally overpriced offers so that the contract could go to the “predetermined” company. The company that was meant to win the contract was in some cases referred to as the “game leader” or “leader”. This “leader” would then assume the role of organiser and coordinator in implementing the cartel agreement. For example, it was to tell the other companies which prices they should communicate to their customers in fake bids. In exchange for submitting such fake bids, companies usually received subcontracts. Sometimes, however, it was also agreed that the companies not receiving any subcontracts would be given priority in the next equivalent tender. In other cases, in return for submitting an agreed excessively high offer, companies received a planning commission or a commission for an expert report, which, at least in individual cases, was not prepared but was invoiced (so-called compensation business). 3 To this extent, the cartel agreements related to individual project-related tenders. However, compensation between the companies involved in the cartel agreement was not only made in relation to specific projects. Rather, the system was based on a cross-project “understanding and relationship of trust" among the individual companies. In return for submitting a fake bid in a specific project, the “protecting company” could in principle assume that it would be “protected” in turn by the other members of the cartel in another project. The course of proceedings in making agreements was so well-established as a rule of play that frequently an explicit agreement between the participating companies in the respective projects was unnecessary in any individual case. In order to reduce the risk of discovery, there were occasional deviations from these procedures, whereby a company in the cartel was allocated a project for a company for which it was not the regular supplier. In exchange, the regular supplier was subcontracted. The allocation of regular customers to the undertakings was facilitated by certain technical specifications frequently demanded by the customers themselves. The cartel members were often involved in drawing up the specifications of their regular customers’ tenders, enabling them to influence the preparation of the tender documents and product requirements both in technical and planning terms. By combining the regular customer system with specifications of particular products tailored to particular companies, it was clear to individual cartel members even before a tender who should be awarded a particular project by a particular customer. From 2001 to 2008 at least, the meetings of the so-called Marketing Working Group within the German Switch Construction Federation (Fachverband Weichenbau) or the German Railway Industry Association (Verb and der Bahnindustrie - VDB) served cartel members as a special platform for agreements in projects relating mainly to switches. These meetings took place five to eight times a year. From early 2009 onwards, the Working Group became less significant as a forum for agreements between the switch manufacturers. Contacts were now made more frequently in relation to individual cases. This was because the regular customer allocation and the approach it involved had 4 established themselves between the cartel members, taking different forms in different regions. Within the cartel structure described above, there was also a bilateral anti-competitive distribution agreement between Thyssen-Krupp GfT Gleistechnik GmbH and TSTG Schienen Technik GmbH, part of the voestalpine group. This distribution agreement related only to the rail product sector. The second part of the rail cartel proceedings, which are now complete, was no longer about collusive agreements to the detriment of Deutsche Bahn AG. Proceedings relating to these offences were concluded in July 2013 with the imposition of fines against the company Moravia Steel1. Throughout these proceedings, the Bundeskartellamt has cooperated closely with the public prosecutor’s office and the criminal investigation department in Bochum, since they relate to cartels concerning publicly tendered products and services. The public prosecutor’s office is investigating the natural persons involved on suspicion of collusive tendering. 1 Case summary of 14 December 2012 and press release of 11 July 2013)
